Question: What is it like to attend Brigham Young University in Provo, UT?

It can be challenging and rigorous, but at the same time mold you into a better person. Part of the BYU experience will be the people you meet. Lost on campus? Need a hand? Just ask a fellow student. They will be more than happy to help. While BYU is an LDS school, it is much like any other large university, except for the fact that we are stone-cold sober. Instead of alcohol, we stock up on the Creamery’s chocolate milk. If I had to do it all over again, I’d pick BYU hands down. It’s such a special place to me. Go cougars!

Question: Was anyone else a little disappointed in the lightsaber fight between Kylo Ren and Rey?
Answer: I think the lightsaber fight was great. Initially, I was a little disappointed, but after watching the movie three times, I realized how great it was. Firstly, Kylo Ren was shot in the side by Chewie. Ask yourself how many people get shot in the side, and still have enough energy to pursue an enemy, let alone fight. Secondly, let's remember that Rey is extremely powerful in the Force, as seen many times on Starkiller base. Although untrained, a weakened Kylo Ren might not be as formidable an opponent as he would be if he was 100 percent. Remember that Rey is fighting without the pain of a blaster wound. Secondly, during the fight with Finn, Finn managed to land a few lightsaber strikes on Kylo Ren. Again, we see how powerful Ren is. Over the many lightsaber battles, we usually see that one lightsaber strike to the torso is enough to do damage to disarm an opponent, if not maim and kill them. One strike killed Darth Maul, Qui-Gon, disarmed Anakin, Obi-Wan, Dooku, disarmed Anakin again, disarmed Windu and the Jedi trying to arrest Palpy, killed Obi-Wan, dis-armed Luke, and finally disarmed Vader. In fact, I'm pretty sure that Kylo Ren is the first instance of a warrior continuing to fight and winning the duel (against Finn) after being struck with a lightsaber, only taking into account the six movies by George Lucas. Mace Windu tried to parry Palpy's lightning, but only lasted about three seconds before he was zapped (pun intended) into oblivion. True, Kylo Ren didn't get his arm cut off, but a lightsaber strike to the face isn't my idea of a paper cut. Third, Kylo Ren is fighting the demons of light vs dark. After killing his father Han, he was so shocked by what he was done that he might have been weakened by the light still in him, as seen when he gets shot by Chewie. Before he was shot, his facial expression shows the light still left in him. The duel was probably a few minutes after, but again, how many people, good or bad, have the strength to fight a lightsaber battle against two people after losing their father, getting shot, struck by a lightsaber, and in the freezing cold of starkiller base? I know we're talking about Kylo Ren, but it's clear from his facial expressions that his feelings were very much conflicted. And Rey lands a few more strikes on Ren as well, probably because his injuries left him in a weakened state. Yet Ren still slashes and tries to defend himself against the parry of lightsaber slashes by Rey. Although not as spectacular as the Anakin vs Obi Wan duel on Mustafar, the light saber duel on Starkiller base shows a perfect balance between an injured, yet incredibly powerful dark side user, vs a recently discovered force sensitive whose relative skill level is not unlike Luke's at Bespin. Kylo's fight despite his injuries shows how incredibly powerful he is. His injuries put him at a severe handicap, allowing Rey to best him. It shows the arc and the development of two characters who will no doubt become major players in the upcoming episodes of Star Wars. Ernest Hemingway emphasized the theme of less is more, and although this battle is far from being bland, there is much to be implied. Star Wars was never a hands on tell all movie, leaving much to be implied and thought through by the audience. There is so much in the films that it's impossible to catch everything through one or two or even five goes. This light-saber battle is just one of many examples of metaphor in the saga. Although not as spectacular, it was every bit as important as a duel like Anakin vs Obi-Wan or Anakin vs Dooku.

Question: How come the further a planet is away from a star, the colder it becomes?
Answer: The anount of radiation an object receives from a star decreases by the inverse square of the distance it is at. For example, a planet 2 times more distant than the Earth will receive 4 times less total radiation than the Earth does, while an object 3 times closer (Mercury) would receive approximately 9 times the amount of radiation. This means that the further a planet is from a star, the amount of light energy is decreased proportionally. By this same token, the planetary equilibrium temperature of an object would decrease accordingly. The planetary equilibrium temperature is basically what the temperature of the planet would be given amount of starlight and without the effects of atmospheres or albedo. Planetary equilibrium temperature - Wikipedia Of course, given that most planets have atmospheres, the actual temperature of planets can be sometimes very different from the planetary equilibrium temperature. Venus, as an example, has an equilibrium temperature of roughly 227K, but has an actual temperature of nearly 800K! But given the amount of starlight received, it should theoretically have a temperature similar to that of Earth. But oddballs aside, the inverse square law of electromagnetic radiation coupled with the planetary equilibrium should be sufficient in determining roughly how hot a planet should be, minus the effects of a greenhouse.

Question: I am going on a long plane flight for Asia soon. Should I worry about terrorists hijacking the plane?
Answer: The chances of hijacking a plane today is extremely slim. First and foremost, the flight deck door is bullet proof. How anyone would get through that thing is next to impossible. Don't ask me, because other than rushing a pilot when he uses the bathroom, there is next to no chance. Second, if someone caused trouble in he passenger cabin, as a pilot, we'd just lock the door and land the plane. The door is supposed to be locked anyways. Then authorities come onboard and deal with it. When that door is locked, no matter what the guy is doing, he won't bring down the plane unless he has a bomb. But what are the chances of bringing a bomb onboard? Slim to none. True, that Metrojet flight was blown up last year, but it was one out of millions of flights that didn't get bombed. So even if the plane gets hijacked, the pilots can still land safely. Third, security will probably prevent the plane from getting hijacked. Sure, there are loopholes, but as strict as security is these days, any terrorist would have to be either foolhardy or really good at his game to even attempt to do that. The possibility of getting caught is too high. Granted, I'm no terrorist mastermind, but if you get caught, the prospect of life imprisonment plus daily beatdowns in jail doesn't really entice people too much. It's much easier to go someplace else with less security and cause trouble. Of course, someone like a pilot could bypass everything and hijack it from within, but what are the chances of that? It's only happened about 6 or 7 times, and usually by a suicidal pilot, not a jihadi. How many airline pilots would willingly compromise the lives of their passengers? Not many. When we're in that cockpit, it's our duty to protect our passengers as best we can, even if it means forfeiting our own lives. Every one of my pilot friends would agree with that. I think there are better things to worry about than a jihadi terrorizing the flight. Have a seat, look out the window, enjoy the airplane food, watch Star Wars onboard, etc. Worry more about your trip planning or your kids than the possibility of dying due to a terrorist. I give you my word. Everything will be ok. The pilots and flight attendants will keep you safe. You're in good hands.
